properties.natural_language: Log entries received from the transaction execution engine must contain valid 20-byte addresses and 32-byte topics before bloom filter construction begins.
The log tuple provided by the transaction execution engine must be a well-formed sequence of Log objects; malformed log data must not be passed to bloom filter processing.
After bloom filter initialization, the bloom filter must be exactly 256 bytes (2048 bits) with all bits set to zero.
After all logs are processed, the completed bloom filter must have exactly the bits set corresponding to each log address and each log topic, and no other bits may have been cleared.
The bloom filter must always be exactly 256 bytes (2048 bits) throughout the entire construction lifecycle; its size must never change.
Bloom filter bit-setting is monotonic: once a bit is set to 1 during construction, it must never be cleared back to 0.
The 11-bit value extraction from keccak256 hash bytes must use big-endian byte ordering, and the mask 0x07FF must be applied to constrain values to the range [0, 2047].

The keccak256 hash function must produce uniformly distributed outputs sufficient for bloom filter bit distribution; non-uniform distribution degrades search performance but must not affect correctness.
Each bloom entry must result in exactly 3 bit positions being set, derived from byte pairs (0-1), (2-3), and (4-5) of the keccak256 hash.
Client log search queries crossing the trust boundary must contain valid filter addresses (20-byte) and/or valid filter topics (32-byte) before bloom check processing.
A bloom filter check that reports 'no match' must guarantee the block does not contain any matching logs (zero false negatives). A 'possibly matches' result may include false positives.
The EVM stack must contain at least 2 elements before KECCAK256 opcode execution begins; otherwise a StackUnderflowError must be raised.
Gas must be sufficient to cover GAS_KECCAK256 (30) + GAS_KECCAK256_WORD (6) * ceil(size/32) + memory expansion cost before KECCAK256 hash computation proceeds.
After KECCAK256 execution, the stack must contain exactly one more element than after the two pops, and that element must be the 32-byte keccak256 hash of the memory region.
After KECCAK256 execution, the program counter must be incremented by exactly 1.
Word count calculation must use ceiling division: words = ceil(size / 32). Non-multiple-of-32 sizes must round up to the next whole word.
Memory read operations during KECCAK256 must only access the EVM's internal memory space; out-of-bounds access must never occur after memory expansion.
If gas is insufficient for KECCAK256 execution, the operation must revert with OutOfGasError and must not produce any hash result or modify the stack.
After memory expansion, newly allocated memory must be initialized to zero bytes and the memory size must be rounded up to the nearest 32-byte word boundary.
The Keccak-256 implementation must be cryptographically secure and produce deterministic 32-byte outputs for identical inputs across all implementations.
External debugging tools setting custom tracers must provide a valid EvmTracer implementation conforming to the __call__ protocol before tracer installation.
External debugging tools must not provide tracer implementations that modify EVM execution state; tracers must be read-only observers.
Every TransactionStart event must be paired with exactly one TransactionEnd event; trace events must maintain strict start/end bracketing.
Every OpStart event must be followed by either an OpEnd event (normal completion) or an OpException event (error), but not both.
When the default (no-op) tracer is active, all trace events must be silently discarded without any performance overhead or side effects.
After set_evm_trace is called, the previously active tracer must be returned to the caller and the new tracer must be installed as the active tracer.
Custom tracer callbacks must execute within bounded time and must not significantly delay EVM execution; slow tracers must not cause transaction timeouts.

Trace data exposed to external tracer implementations crosses a trust boundary; the tracer has read access to sensitive EVM state (stack, memory, storage) and this data may be leaked, logged, or transmitted.
Trace data exposed to external tracers must follow EIP-3155 format standards to ensure compatibility with existing debugging and analysis tools.
Wallet/signer creating transactions must include a valid non-zero CHAIN_ID in the signing data to enable replay protection.
Transaction data from the wallet must include exactly six base fields (nonce, gasprice, startgas, to, value, data) before signing data preparation.
After EIP-155 signing, the v parameter must equal {0,1} + CHAIN_ID * 2 + 35, ensuring the chain ID is recoverable from the signature.
After signing data preparation, the RLP encoding must contain exactly nine elements: the six transaction fields followed by CHAIN_ID, 0, 0.
Signed transactions received from the broadcast network must contain a valid v, r, s signature tuple before validation processing begins.
Transactions with v values that do not match expected patterns (27, 28, or CHAIN_ID*2+35/36) must be rejected as malformed.
For EIP-155 format transactions, the extracted CHAIN_ID = (v - 35) / 2 must match the current network's CHAIN_ID; mismatches must result in transaction rejection.
Each Ethereum-compatible chain must use a unique CHAIN_ID value; CHAIN_ID=0 must be treated as invalid and rejected.
An EIP-155 signed transaction valid on chain A must be rejected on chain B if the chains have different CHAIN_IDs, preventing cross-chain replay attacks.
Legacy transactions (v=27/28) lack chain replay protection and may be valid on multiple chains; this must be treated as a known security limitation.
The nine-element hashing requirement in EIP-155 signing SHOULD be treated as mandatory for security purposes; non-compliant implementations are vulnerable to replay attacks.
Calling contracts invoking the RIPEMD-160 precompile at address 0x03 must provide input data via evm.message.data; the precompile must accept arbitrary-length input including empty input.
The RIPEMD-160 precompile must always produce a 20-byte digest that is left-padded with 12 zero bytes to yield exactly 32 bytes of output.
The RIPEMD-160 precompile output must always be exactly 32 bytes, with the first 12 bytes being zero and the last 20 bytes being the hash digest.
Gas must be sufficient to cover GAS_RIPEMD160 (base) + GAS_RIPEMD160_WORD * ceil32(len(data))/32 before the hash computation proceeds.
If gas is insufficient during base or per-word charging, the precompile must terminate with an out-of-gas error without producing any output.
The RIPEMD-160 hash implementation must produce cryptographically correct and deterministic outputs; finding collisions must be computationally infeasible.
The RIPEMD-160 precompile must always be available at address 0x03 on mainnet and compatible chains; unavailability would break Bitcoin-Ethereum bridge contracts.
Announcement metadata (address, nonce) received from peer nodes is UNVERIFIED and must never be used for security-critical decisions such as access control or rate limiting.
Incoming 0x08 NewPooledTransactionHashes messages from peers must be parsed to extract hash, type, size, address, and nonce; malformed messages must be rejected.
Announcement metadata must only be used as an optimization hint for request prioritization, never to filter out transactions entirely based on sender address (which constitutes censorship).
After retrieving a full transaction, the announced metadata (hash, type, size, address, nonce) must be validated against the actual transaction; mismatches must flag the peer as a protocol violator.
Malicious nodes can send arbitrary false announcement metadata without cryptographic proof; the system must remain correct regardless of the truthfulness of announcement data.
Protocol violation handling must maintain a violation counter per peer; peers exceeding a threshold must be disconnected to prevent abuse.
The additional message size (B_20 address + nonce per transaction) must not create a DoS vector; announcement message processing must be bounded in time and resources.
DNS TXT records received from the DNS resolver are untrusted and must be validated via signature verification against the known secp256k1 public key before any node data is used.
The enrtree URL provided via client configuration must contain a valid base32-encoded secp256k1 public key; malformed URLs must be rejected.
DNS TXT records from the resolver must be validated for format, and entries exceeding 512 bytes must be rejected as invalid per UDP DNS limits.
After root signature verification fails, the discovery process must halt and no node records from this tree must be imported.
Sequence numbers in root records must be monotonically non-decreasing; a sequence number lower than the previously cached value indicates a potential replay attack and must be rejected.
Branch entry content must be verified via keccak256 hash comparison against the subdomain name; hash mismatches indicate corruption and must cause the entry to be rejected.
Clients must use multiple independent DNS discovery sources to mitigate eclipse attacks; reliance on a single publisher allows that publisher to restrict visible nodes.
Attackers must not be able to forge signatures matching the publisher's secp256k1 public key; the security of the entire DNS discovery scheme relies on this cryptographic assumption.
The wallet_getOwnedAssets request from a dApp must contain a valid Ethereum address parameter; invalid address formats must be rejected with a standard JSON-RPC error.
Before returning asset data, the wallet must obtain explicit user consent through a consent dialog; the system must never silently expose asset information to dApps.
All request parameters (address, chainId, limit, types) must pass validation before any asset query is executed; invalid parameters must return appropriate error codes.
If the user denies the asset sharing request, the wallet must return an empty or error response to the dApp and must not leak any asset information.
Only assets explicitly whitelisted by the user for a specific dApp may be included in responses; the wallet must never return non-whitelisted assets.
An attacker must not be able to spoof a dApp's identity to gain unauthorized access to user asset information; dApp identity must be verified before consent flow.
The wallet must accurately report asset ownership and balances; the response data must reflect current on-chain state at the latest block.
Transaction calldata submitted by external entities must be processed byte-by-byte for gas calculation; each byte must be classified as zero (0x00) or non-zero.
Zero bytes in calldata must cost exactly 4 gas each; non-zero bytes must cost exactly 16 gas each (reduced from 68 per EIP-2028).
Transaction gas limit must be greater than or equal to the intrinsic gas (base cost + calldata gas) before the transaction can be accepted for execution.
If the transaction gas limit is less than the calculated intrinsic gas, the transaction must be rejected and not included in any block.
Network block propagation delay must remain within acceptable bounds per the Sompolinsky-Zohar security model despite increased effective block sizes from cheaper calldata.
Block producers must not be able to exploit cheap calldata to create blocks that propagate so slowly as to gain competitive advantage through selfish mining.
EIP-2028 calldata gas pricing applies only to traditional calldata; blob data (EIP-4844) has separate pricing and must not be confused with calldata.
Contract bytecode submitted by deployers must be checked for the EOF magic prefix (0xEF00) to determine format; all EOF-prefixed bytecode must pass full container validation before deployment.
EOF initcode containers submitted for contract creation must pass validation before execution; invalid initcode must cause creation failure.
After EOF structure validation passes, code section validation must verify all opcodes are valid per EIP-3670; invalid opcodes must prevent deployment.
After initcode execution, the generated deployed code must also pass EOF validation; invalid deployed code must cause contract creation to fail.
Static stack validation at deploy time must guarantee that no runtime stack underflow or overflow can occur in any execution path of the code section.
An attacker must not be able to craft EOF bytecode that passes deploy-time validation but exhibits exploitable behavior at runtime.
The EVM stack must never exceed 1024 items during EOF code execution; this limit must be enforced statically during deployment validation.
CALLF must push a return address onto the return stack before transferring execution to the target code section; RETF must pop and restore the caller's execution context.
JUMPF (tail call) must transfer execution to the target section without pushing a return address; the return stack must not grow from JUMPF operations.
Legacy contracts must continue to function alongside EOF contracts; cross-contract calls between legacy and EOF formats must not fail due to format incompatibility.
